title: In Turkish ebru, a pattern is painted on water first
body: An ebru artist drops or brushes pigment onto a prepared bath. The colours float and can be shaped on the surface. The artist then lowers a sheet of paper onto the design to take an impression.
takeaway: The liquid surface acts as a temporary printing plate that is rebuilt for every sheet.
visual: swirled pigment floating in a shallow tray with paper poised above it

title: Chinese tea makers distinguish six broad categories of tea
body: UNESCO's 2022 listing for China's traditional tea processing names green, white, yellow, oolong, black and dark teas. Local practices for processing leaves create distinct categories as well as many individual varieties.
takeaway: The variety comes partly from what people do after the leaf is picked.
source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Traditional Tea Processing in China (2022)
visual: small piles of differently prepared tea leaves in a row on a dark wooden table

title: Ladakh's monasteries preserve sacred texts through chanting
body: Buddhist monks in Ladakh recite sacred texts in a practice UNESCO listed in 2012. Chanting is used in monasteries and village settings, with styles that vary between traditions.
takeaway: A text preserved in sound can be passed on through listening and practice as well as through reading.
source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Buddhist Chanting of Ladakh (2012)
visual: a group of robed monks seated in a Ladakhi monastery hall
